name: SAP
summary: SAP makes enterprise software, best known for ERP, that companies use to run finance, supply chain, procurement and HR. Its careers site says that, depending on the role, the process may include recruiter and hiring manager interviews and technical or behavioural assessments. For campus and early-career engineering roles, including at SAP Labs India, candidates commonly report an online coding and aptitude test followed by technical and HR interviews.
rounds: Application review by the recruiting team
Online test for many campus and early-career roles: coding and aptitude
Technical interviews, often one or two: coding, computer science fundamentals and your projects
Hiring manager interview on your experience, motivation and fit with the team
looks_for: Strong fundamentals: data structures, object-oriented design, databases and operating systems
Understanding of how businesses run: orders, invoices, stock, payroll
Building reliable, secure software for business customers
Working well across teams and countries
Curiosity and willingness to learn new tools, including cloud and AI
Honesty about what you know and don't know

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to understand how a business process worked before you could build software for it.
covers: The process and the people who used it
How you learned it: questions, shadowing users, reading data
How that understanding changed what you built

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with a teammate in another country or time zone. What made it work?
covers: The task and how the work was split
What was hard: overlap hours, language, different habits
The habits that helped and the result

questions.text: Tell me about a commitment to a teammate or customer that became hard to keep. What did you do?
covers: What you promised and what changed
When and how you told the other person
What you delivered, and what you'd promise differently next time

questions.text: Tell me about a piece of feedback that changed how you work.
covers: The feedback and who gave it
Your first reaction, honestly
What you changed and how you know it helped

questions.text: Explain what an ERP system does, using a company that sells and ships products as your example.
covers: One shared system for finance, sales, stock, buying and people
Following one order through: sale, stock, delivery, invoice, payment
Why one system beats many separate tools: one version of the truth

questions.text: How would you design an order-to-cash flow, from a customer placing an order to the company receiving payment?
covers: The main steps and the data each one needs
Where things go wrong: credit checks, partial deliveries, returns
How you'd keep the steps consistent and leave an audit trail

questions.text: What's the difference between a process and a thread, and when would you use multiple threads?
covers: Processes have their own memory; threads share their process's memory
Using threads for parallel or waiting work, such as handling many requests
The risks: race conditions and deadlocks, and how locks help

questions.text: Explain how a database index speeds up queries, and what it costs.
covers: An index works like a book's index, often a B-tree, so lookups skip a full scan
The cost: extra storage and slower inserts and updates
Choosing columns to index from the queries you actually run

questions.text: A customer says month-end reports in their finance system have become very slow. How would you investigate?
covers: Scope first: which reports, since when, after what change
Checking data growth, slow queries and missing indexes
A quick relief for month-end and a lasting fix after

questions.text: What changes when a company moves a large business application from its own servers to the cloud? Talk me through the main risks.
covers: Gains: scaling, updates, less hardware to run
Risks: data migration, downtime, security and custom code that breaks
Moving in stages with testing and a way back

questions.text: Walk me through your best project: what you built, the hardest bug and what you'd do differently.
covers: The problem and your part in a few sentences
The hardest bug and how you tracked it down
What you'd change in the design now

questions.text: Why SAP, and which of its products or business areas interests you most?
covers: Something specific about SAP's software or customers
The area you chose and why it fits your skills
What you want to learn in your first year

questions.text: SAP's customers are mostly businesses, not consumers. Why does building that kind of software appeal to you?
covers: What's interesting about business software: scale, complexity, real impact
An example of a business problem software solved well
Why you'd enjoy working on it

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in five years?
covers: A realistic direction, technical or towards leading people
Skills you plan to build on the way
How this role fits that path

tips: Learn how a business runs day to day: a sale, an invoice, a stock movement, a payslip. SAP's software is built around these flows.
Revise core subjects (data structures, OOP, databases, operating systems, networks); campus technical rounds commonly test them.
Know one project end to end, including design choices and how you tested it; interviewers often go deep on one project.
SAP's careers site prefers applications in English and lets you apply to several roles; pick the ones that genuinely match your skills.
If you're early in your career, look at the academies on SAP's careers site; each has its own focus, such as product and engineering or customer success.
